title: Managing a Python Installation
section: The Golden Rule of Python Environments
text:
The Golden Rule of Python Environments
When you want to install a package for Python (like pandas), many guides often tell you to open the terminal and type pip install pandas. Do not do this.
Operating systems like MacOS and Linux rely on a hidden, system-level Python installation to run core operating system background tasks. If you use global pip to install or upgrade packages, you risk overwriting the dependencies your operating system relies on. This leads to a broken OS, or at best, conflicting dependencies between your own projects (often called “Dependency Hell”).
Preventing Dependecy Hell: Every project must live in its own isolated “Virtual Environment.”
This is one of the downsides to Python, in order to prevent dependency conflicts you need to manage what amounts to different Python installations. Fortunately, there are solutions that make this less tedious and prone to complication.

title: Managing a Python Installation
text:
uv
Historically, managing Python safely required juggling several different tools (pyenv for Python versions, venv for environments, pip for packages, and pipx for global apps).
There are multiple solutions to managing different Python installations (Conda/Miniconda are very popular), a recent one is uv. This replaces all of the traditional tools with a single tool. It operates entirely in user-space, meaning it requires no administrator privileges and generally can be installed without friction on computers that you do not have full control over.

1. Installing uv
Open your terminal and run the official standalone installer:
# On macOS/Linux
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

# On Windows
powershell -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | more"


2. Installing Python Versions
You do not need to download Python from the official website. uv will download and isolate whatever version of Python you need for a project.
For example, if you need a Python version of 3.12 as a requirement:
# Install the latest version of Python 3.12
uv python install 3.12


3. Creating a Project
When creating a new project, uv makes environment isolation automatic.
# Create a new project directory
mkdir data_analysis_project
cd data_analysis_project

# Initialize the project structure
uv init

# Add a package (this automatically creates the virtual environment!)
uv add pandas matplotlib
Notice that we never had to manually “activate” an environment. By using uv add, the tool automatically handles the creation and linkage of the isolated environment.


4. Running Your Code
To run a script using the isolated environment, simply prefix your command with uv run.
# Runs script.py using the isolated pandas/matplotlib installation
uv run script.py

title: Managing a Python Installation
text:
Installing Global Tools
Sometimes you need to install a Python application that you want to use everywhere, not just in one project. A good example is something like Jupyter Lab.
Installing an application into a specific project’s virtual environment is tedious, but installing them globally via pip breaks the Golden Rule.
The solution is an isolated tool runner.
# Install Jupyter Lab in its own isolated global environment
uv tool install jupyterlab

# You can now launch Jupyter from anywhere on your computer
jupyter lab
If you are working on a legacy system without uv, the traditional equivalent of this command is pipx install jupyterlab.

title: Managing a Python Installation
text:
Working with Older Codebases
While uv is the modern standard, you will inevitably encounter older codebases or tutorials that use the standard library tools. Adjusting them to use uv is straightforward.
If a repository contains a requirements.txt file, the traditional setup workflow looks like this:

Create the Environment:

python3 -m venv .venv

Activate the Environment: (You must do this every time you open a new terminal)

# macOS / Linux
source .venv/bin/activate

# Windows
.venv\Scripts\activate

Install the Dependencies:

pip install -r requirements.txt

Deactivate:

deactivate

title: Managing a Python Installation
text:
Recap
Need a library for a script? (e.g., numpy, pandas) -> Use uv add or a local venv.
Need a standalone app? (e.g., jupyter) -> Use uv tool install or pipx.
Never use: pip install [package] outside of an active virtual environment.

section: Types of Files and File Access Methods
text:
Types of Files and File Access Methods

In general, two types of files

Text file: contains data that has been encoded as text
Binary file: contains data that has not been converted to text

Two ways to access data stored in file

Sequential access: file read sequentially from beginning to end, can’t skip ahead
Direct access: can jump directly to any piece of data in the file

title: 13: Exceptions and Files
text:
Filenames and File Objects (1 of 2)

Filename extensions: short sequences of characters that appear at the end of a filename preceded by a period

Extension indicates type of data stored in the file

File object: object associated with a specific file

Provides a way for a program to work with the file: file object referenced by a variable

title: 13: Exceptions and Files
text:
Opening a File

open function: used to open a file

Creates a file object and associates it with a file on the disk
General format:
file_object = open(filename, mode)

Mode: string specifying how the file will be opened

Example: reading only (‘r’), writing (‘w’), and appending (‘a’)

title: 13: Exceptions and Files
section: Specifying the Location of a File
text:
Specifying the Location of a File

If open function receives a filename that does not contain a path, assumes that file is in same directory as program
If program is running and file is created, it is created in the same directory as the program

Can specify alternative path and file name in the open function argument

Prefix the path string literal with the letter r

title: 13: Exceptions and Files
text:
Writing Data to a File

Method: a function that belongs to an object

Performs operations using that object

File object’s write method used to write data to the file

Format: file_variable.write(string)

File should be closed using file object close method

Format: file_variable.close()

title: 13: Exceptions and Files
text:
Reading Data From a File

read method: file object method that reads entire file contents into memory

Only works if file has been opened for reading
Contents returned as a string

readline method: file object method that reads a line from the file

Line returned as a string, including ‘\n’

Read position: marks the location of the next item to be read from a file

title: 13: Exceptions and Files
section: Concatenating a Newline to and Stripping it From a String
text:
Concatenating a Newline to and Stripping it From a String

In most cases, data items written to a file are values referenced by variables

Usually necessary to concatenate a ‘\n’ to data before writing it

Carried out using the + operator in the argument of the write method


In many cases need to remove ‘\n’ from string after it is read from a file

rstrip method: string method that strips specific characters from end of the string

title: 13: Exceptions and Files
section: Appending Data to an Existing File
text:
Appending Data to an Existing File

When open file with ‘w’ mode, if the file already exists it is overwritten
To append data to a file use the ‘a’ mode

If file exists, it is not erased, and if it does not exist it is created
Data is written to the file at the end of the current contents

title: 13: Exceptions and Files
text:
Writing and Reading Numeric Data

Numbers must be converted to strings before they are written to a file
str function: converts value to string
Number are read from a text file as strings

Must be converted to numeric type in order to perform mathematical operations
Use int and float functions to convert string to numeric value

title: 13: Exceptions and Files
text:
Using Loops to Process Files

Files typically used to hold large amounts of data

Loop typically involved in reading from and writing to a file

Often the number of items stored in file is unknown

The readline method uses an empty string as a sentinel when end of file is reached

Can write a while loop with the condition



while line != ’’

section: Figure 6-17 General Logic for Detecting the End of a File
text:
Figure 6-17 General Logic for Detecting the End of a File
A flowchart depicts the logic to detect the end of a file. For long description in Notes pane, press F6.

The flow is as follows. The process enters open the file that points to use read line to read the first line from the file. Then the process enters a decision, did read line return an empty string. If yes, true, close the file. If no, false, process the item that was just read from the file and then use read line to read the next line from the file. After this, the process again enters the decision symbol.

title: 13: Exceptions and Files
section: Using Python’s for Loop to Read Lines
text:
Using Python’s for Loop to Read Lines

Python allows the programmer to write a for loop that automatically reads lines in a file and stops when end of file is reached

Format: for line in file_object:
statements
The loop iterates once over each line in the file

for i in range(1, 6):

Then append the values within the list (each independent value, not the entire list at once) to the file example2.txt

title: 13: Exceptions and Files

Combining Reading and Writing

The + symbol adds reading and writing to a file mode.
‘r+’ → read and write

File must already exist
File pointer starts at the beginning
Writing happens at the current file position

title: 13: Exceptions and Files
text:
Combining Reading and Writing

The + symbol adds reading and writing to a file mode.

‘r+’ → read and write (file must already exist)

File must already exist
File pointer starts at the beginning
Writing happens at the current file position
Writing can overwrite existing content


‘w+’ → write and read (file is cleared first)
‘a+’ → append and read (writing goes to the end)

title: 13: Exceptions and Files
text:
Combining Reading and Writing

‘w+’ → write and read

Deletes all existing contents when the file is opened
If the file does not exist, it creates it
File position starts at the beginning

‘a+’ → append and read

File is created if it does not exist
File pointer starts at the end
Writing always adds to the end
Reading requires moving the file pointer manually

Lines are successfully written to the file
The file pointer is now at the end
The read loop starts at the end
Result: Nothing is printed

title: 13: Exceptions and Files
text:
File Pointer

Python keeps track of the current location we are at in the file using a file pointer.
So, to read what was just written, we must move the file pointer:
We can do this by: file.seek(0)
seek(0) moves the pointer to the start of the file

Now reading will work as expected in our previous example

title: 13: Exceptions and Files
section: Example – Reading and Writing to a File
text:
Example – Reading and Writing to a File
file = open(“example.txt”, “a+“)
for i in range(1, 6):
file.write(f”Line {i}\n”)
file.seek(0)
for line in file:
print(line.rstrip(‘\n’))
file.close()

What happens:
Lines are successfully written to the file
The file pointer is now at the end
We move the file pointer to the beginning using file.seek(0)
The read loop starts at the beginning
The output is now the expected “Line 1” … “Line 5”


Without the rstrip, we would have an extra newline for every printed line.

title: 13: Exceptions and Files
section: Using the with Statement to Open Files (1 of 4)
text:
Using the with Statement to Open Files (1 of 4)

The with statement can be used to open a file and automatically close the file. General format:

with open(filename, mode) as file_variable:
statement
statement
etc.

filename is a string specifying the name of the file
mode is a string specifying the mode, such as ‘r’, ‘w’, or ‘a’
file_variable is the name of the variable that will reference the file object
The indented block of statements is known as the with suite

title: 13: Exceptions and Files
section: Using the with Statement to Open Files (2 of 4)
text:
Using the with Statement to Open Files (2 of 4)

Example:

with open(‘myfile.txt’, ‘w’) as output_file:
statement
statement
etc.

This example opens a file named myfile.txt
Code inside the with suite can use output_file to write data to the file
When the code inside the with suite has finished, the file is automatically closed

title: 13: Exceptions and Files
section: Using the with Statement to Open Files (3 of 4)
text:
Using the with Statement to Open Files (3 of 4)

Example:

with open(‘myfile.txt’, ‘r’) as input_file:
statement
statement

Code inside the with suite can use input_file to read data from the file
When the code inside the with suite has finished, the file is automatically closed

title: 13: Exceptions and Files
section: Using the with Statement to Open Files (4 of 4)
text:
Using the with Statement to Open Files (4 of 4)

Opening multiple files with a with statement:

with open(‘file1.txt’, ‘r’) as input_file,
open(‘file2.txt’, ‘w’) as output_file:
statement
statement
etc.

This example opens a file named file1.txt for reading, and a file named file2.txt for writing
Code inside the with suite can use input_file to read data from file1.txt and output_file to write data to file2.txt
When the code inside the with suite has finished, both files are automatically closed

title: 13: Exceptions and Files
text:
Exceptions (1 of 4)

Exception: error that occurs while a program is running

Usually causes program to abruptly halt

Traceback: error message that gives information regarding line numbers that caused the exception

Indicates the type of exception and brief description of the error that caused exception to be raised

title: 13: Exceptions and Files
text:
Exceptions (2 of 4)

Many exceptions can be prevented by careful coding

Example: input validation
Usually involve a simple decision construct

Some exceptions cannot be avoided by careful coding

Examples

Trying to convert non-numeric string to an integer
Trying to open for reading a file that doesn’t exist

title: 13: Exceptions and Files
text:
Exceptions (3 of 4)

Exception handler: code that responds when exceptions are raised and prevents program from crashing

In Python, written as try/except statement

General format: try:



statements
except exceptionName:
statements

Try suite: statements that can potentially raise an exception
Handler: statements contained in except block

title: 13: Exceptions and Files
text:
Exceptions (4 of 4)

If statement in try suite raises exception:

Exception specified in except clause:

Handler immediately following except clause executes
Continue program after try/except statement

Other exceptions:

Program halts with traceback error message


If no exception is raised, handlers are skipped

title: 13: Exceptions and Files
section: Displaying an Exception’s Default Error Message
text:
Displaying an Exception’s Default Error Message

Exception object: object created in memory when an exception is thrown

Usually contains default error message pertaining to the exception
Can assign the exception object to a variable in an except clause

Example: except ValueError as err:

Can pass exception object variable to print function to display the default error message

title: 13: Exceptions and Files
text:
Example
print(variable)
print(“Continuing on”)
> NameError: name ‘variable’ is not defined

text:
Example
try:
print(variable)
except NameError as e:
print(e)
print(“Continuing on”)

text:
Practice

Given the list [1,2,’3’,4,’5’,6], use a for loop to attempt to add each element into an accumulator variable.
Use exception handling (use TypeError as the exception type) to ignore errors for undefined operations.


var = [1,2,‘3’,4,‘5’,6]
s = 0

s += i

title: 13: Exceptions and Files
text:
Handling Multiple Exceptions

Often code in the try suite can throw more than one type of exception

Need to write except clause for each type of exception that needs to be handled

An except clause that does not list a specific exception will handle any exception that is raised in the try suite

Should always be last in a series of except clauses

title: 13: Exceptions and Files
text:
Example
try:
num = int(input())
result = 10 / num
print(result)
except ValueError:
print(”Invalid Number.”)
except ZeroDivisionError:
print(”Zero Division.”)

We can catch two specific errors here:
ValueError: input is not a number
ZeroDivisionError: user enters 0
Each error is handled separately

title: 13: Exceptions and Files
text:
Example
try:
num = int(input())
result = 10 / num
print(result)
except:
print(“An error occurred.”)

This handles all exceptions
But it does not tell you what went wrong
This format is considered bad form
Always use specific exceptions when possible

title: 13: Exceptions and Files
text:
Example
try:
num = int(input())
result = 10 / num
print(result)
except ValueError:
print(”Invalid Number.”)
except ZeroDivisionError:
print(”Zero Division.”)
except:
print(“An error occurred.”)

Python checks except clauses top to bottom
A generic except would catch everything if placed first

Specific error handling would never run

title: 13: Exceptions and Files
text:
The else Clause

try/except statement may include an optional else clause, which appears after all the except clauses

Aligned with try and except clauses
Syntax similar to else clause in decision structure
Else suite: block of statements executed after statements in try suite, only if no exceptions were raised

If exception was raised, the else suite is skipped

title: 13: Exceptions and Files

text:
The finally Clause

try/except statement may include an optional finally clause, which appears after all the except clauses

Aligned with try and except clauses
General format: finally:


statements

Finally suite: block of statements after the finally clause

Execute whether an exception occurs or not
Purpose is to perform cleanup before exiting

text:
What If an Exception Is Not Handled?

Two ways for exception to go unhandled:

No except clause specifying exception of the right type
Exception raised outside a try suite

In both cases, exception will cause the program to halt

Python documentation provides information about exceptions that can be raised by different functions

title: 11: Dictionaries
text:
Dictionaries
Dictionaries are another type of object that stores a collection of data. What makes them different from the other data structures we have seen so far is that each element is actually two parts: a key and a value.

Often referred to as mapping of key to value
Key must be an immutable object like an integer or a string

To retrieve a specific value, we use the key associated with it.
The format for creating a dictionary is: dictionary= {key1:val1, key2:val2}

# Creating a dictionary with fruit names as keys and quantities as values

fruit_counts = {
"apple": 4,
"banana": 2,
"cherry": 10
}

title: 11: Dictionaries
section: Adding Elements to an Existing Dictionary
text:
Adding Elements to an Existing Dictionary

Dictionaries are mutable objects
To add a new key-value pair: dictionary[key] = value
If key exists in the dictionary, the value associated with it will be changed


fruit_counts = {
"apple": 4,
"banana": 2,
"cherry": 10
}

fruit_counts['mango'] = 5

print(fruit_counts)

If key is not in the dictionary, KeyError exception is raised


fruit_counts = {
"apple": 4,
"banana": 2,
"cherry": 10
}

del fruit_counts['cherry']

print(fruit_counts)

section: Creating an Empty Dictionary and Using for Loop to Iterate Over a Dictionary
text:
Creating an Empty Dictionary and Using for Loop to Iterate Over a Dictionary

To create an empty dictionary:

Use {}
Use built-in function dict()
Elements can be added to the dictionary as program executes

Use a for loop to iterate over a dictionary

General format: for key in dictionary



fruit_counts = {
"apple": 4,

}

for key in fruit_counts:

title: 11: Dictionaries
text:
Some Common Dictionary Methods

clear method: deletes all the elements in a dictionary, leaving it empty

Format: dictionary.clear()

get method: gets a value associated with specified key from the dictionary

Format: dictionary.get(key, default)

default is returned if key is not found

Alternative to [] operator

Cannot raise KeyError exception




fruit_counts = {
"apple": 4,
"banana": 2,
"cherry": 10
}

print(fruit_counts.get('mango',-1))

-1



items method: returns all the dictionaries keys and associated values

Format: dictionary.items()
Returned as a dictionary view

Each element in dictionary view is a tuple which contains a key and its associated value
Use a for loop to iterate over the tuples in the sequence

Can use a variable which receives a tuple, or can use two variables which receive key and value





fruit_counts = {
"apple": 4,
"banana": 2,
"cherry": 10
}

for key, value in fruit_counts.items():
  print(key, value, end='\t')

apple 4 banana 2    cherry 10   



keys method: returns all the dictionaries keys as a sequence

Format: dictionary.keys()

pop method: returns value associated with specified key and removes that key-value pair from the dictionary

Format: dictionary.pop(key, default)

5: Functions
text:
We have used prebuilt functions repeatedly in this course (like print or input) and now we will look at building our own.
A function is a group of statements within a program that performs a specific task. This collection of statements is attached to a name, and the name can be used to perform those statements repeatedly without having to duplicate the underlying code.
This idea of code reuse is a primary benefit of functions. We get to write the code once then call it as many times as needed. This appreciably simplifies our codebase as it reduces duplicate code and this results in superior testing and debugged as we only need to test and debug just a single block of code, the function itself.


Function naming rules are very similar to those of variables:

Cannot use keywords as a function name
Cannot contain spaces
First character must be a letter or underscore
All other characters must be a letter, number or underscore
Uppercase and lowercase characters are distinct

And like variables, the function name should be descriptive of the task carried out by the function.




Defining a function:
def function_name(parameter_1,parameter_2, ...):
    statement_1
    statement_2
    ...

The function header is the first line of the function and includes the keyword def and the name of the function. This is followed by parentheses where the (optional) parameters needed by the function are placed and then ended with a colon.
Inside the function we have the statement or statements that you want the function to perform. Note that the statements inside the function must be indented.



To use a function, we call it by invoking its name.

def add(x,y):
    print(x + y)

add(2,3)

5


The simple function add above takes in two parameters, x and y then prints their summed value. A parameter is a variable that is assigned the value of an argument when the function is called. We call the function with specific values for the parameters, arguments, in this case 2 and 3 using the notation add(2,3). Note that the function assigns the parameter values in order of the arguments that are passed in. 2 is the first argument, so it is assigned to x and 3 is the second argument so it is assigned to y.
Functions can take in multiple arguments, a single argument or none at all. How many parameters are needed for a function is dependent on its construction.



The function we just saw does not return any data back out of the function, it simply prints a value to the terminal. We call this type of function that executes the statements it contains and then ends a void function.
In contrast, a value-returning function executes its statements and then returns some value back to the point of the program that called it. The input and int functions are example of value-returning functions that you have used.
To return a value from a function, you need only use the return keyword.

def add(x,y):
    return x + y

result = add(2,3)
print(result)

5


We can see in the modified version of our add function that we now return the sum of the values instead of printing to the terminal. This returned value is stored in the result variable and then this variable is printed to the terminal. Note that we do not need to tell Python what type of value is being returned unlike in some other programming languages. The return keyword only specifics to send that value back, there is no check to see what type of value it actually is.


We can return multiple values by separating the values by commas.

def add(x,y):
    return x + y, x, y

result = add(2,3)
print(result)

(5, 2, 3)


Our add function now returns the sum, then the value associated with parameter x and finally the value associated with parameter y. Note that the values are returned in the order they are specified. Also note that the variable result is now a tuple containing three objects, which is what we would expect since we returned three individual values.
We can assign these values immediately using the convention for multiple assignment:

def add(x,y):
    return x + y, x, y

result, x, y = add(2,3)
print(result)
print(x)
print(y)

5
2
3


If you choose to do multiple assignment from a function call, you will need exactly as many variables as there are returned values.



You can use the pass keyword to create empty functions. This keyword is ignored by the Python interpreter and this can be helpful when designing a program.

def a_function():
    pass





Changes made to a parameter value within the function do not affect the argument. This is known as pass by value and it provides a way for unidirectional communication between one function and another function.

def function_1():
    value = 5
    print(f'The value is {value}')
    function_2(value)
    print(f'The value is {value}')

def function_2(x):
    print(f'The value is {x}')
    x = 0
    print(f'The value is now {x}')

Note that in this example the value in the first function is passed to the second function, but the change is not reflected in the first function. The second function gets a copy of data in the first value and not the actual variable itself.


A keyword argument is an argument that specifies which parameter the value should be passed to.
function_name(parameter=value)
Note that the position when calling the function is not relevant. It is also possible to mix keyword arguments and positional arguments when calling a function but all positional arguments must appear first.
Keyword arguments are often used to provide a default argument for a parameter. A default argument is a value that will be there by default unless explicitly overwritten when the function is called.
In the following example we can omit passing a value into the tax rate parameter because a default argument is provided. We are still free to overwrite it whenever we need.

def show_tax(price, tax_rate=0.08):
    tax = price * tax_rate
    print(f'The tax is {tax}.')

show_tax(10)

show_tax(10,tax_rate=0.10)

The tax is 0.8.
The tax is 1.0.






In Python, scope determines the visibility and lifetime of a variable. That is, scope is the part of a program in which a variable may be accessed.
Python follows the LEGB rule, which defines the order in which the interpreter searches for a variable name.

Local
Enclosing
Global
Built-in



A local variable is variable that is assigned a value inside a function. It belongs to the function in which it was created.
Only statements inside that function can access it, an error will occur if another function tries to access the variable. The scope of a local variable is the function where it was created and any local variables are destroyed when their associated function ends.
A local variable cannot be accessed by statements inside its function which precede its creation. You also cannot access a local variable after the function ends as it no longer exists.
Note that because the scope of a local variable is constrained to its associated function, different functions may have local variables with the same name. Each function does not see the other function’s local variables, so there is no ambiguity to the Python interpreter.
def my_func():
    x = 10  # Local scope
    print(x)

my_func()
# print(x)  # Throws NameError: name 'x' is not defined
Notice how in the example below that despite having the same name, the variables in function 1 and function 2 are different.

x = 10

def function_1():
        x = 4
        print(x)

def function_2():
        print(x)

function_1()
function_2()

4
10





Enclosing (or nonlocal) scope occurs in nested functions. It represents the scope of the outer (enclosing) function from the perspective of the inner function.
By default, an inner function can read variables in the enclosing scope, but attempting to modify them will create a new local variable in the inner function instead. You must use the nonlocal keyword if you intend to mutate an enclosing variable.
However, heavy use of nested functions and nonlocal state can make code difficult to debug and reason about.

def outer_function():
    message = "Hello"  # Enclosing scope
    
    def inner_function():
        nonlocal message
        message = "Hi"  # Modifies the enclosing variable
        
    inner_function()
    print(message)  # Outputs: Hi




Global scope comprises variables defined at the top level of a script, module, or notebook cell. They are accessible anywhere within that specific module. A global variable is created by assignment statement written outside all the functions.
Global variables can be accessed by any statement in the program file, including from within a function. If a function needs to assign a value to the global variable, the global variable must be redeclared within the function.

counter = 0  # Global scope

def increment():
    global counter
    counter += 1

Global variables should generally be avoided as they make debugging difficult. Many portions of the program can change the value of a global variable and as a program becomes larger, finding which location is changing the variable becomes difficult.



Built-in scope is the widest scope. It contains all of Python’s built-in objects, functions, and exceptions (things like print(), len(), list, int, etc.). This scope is automatically loaded whenever you run Python.
Python allows you to reuse built-in names for your own variables like naming a variable list = [1, 2, 3]. This is called shadowing.
sum = 10
a_list = [1,2,3]

print(sum(a_list)) # TypeError: 'int' object is not callable
Once you shadow a built-in name, you lose access to the original built-in function within that scope, which leads to subtle, frustrating bugs later. Always avoid using Python keywords or built-in function names as variable identifiers.




We can differentiate variables that may appear to be the same (by having the same value) using the id() function. The id() function returns a unique identifier, the object’s memory address.

If two variables are stored at the same memory address, they must refer to the same data.
If two variables are stored at different memory addresses, then while they might refer to the same value, they do not refer to the same physical data and so are different to Python.


var1 = 5
var2 = 5

print(f'Var 1 = {id(var1)} \t Var 2 = {id(var2)}')

Var 1 = 4321472608   Var 2 = 4321472608



var1 = 5
var2 = var1

print(f'Var 1 = {id(var1)} \t Var 2 = {id(var2)}')

Var 1 = 4321472608   Var 2 = 4321472608

text:
Recall that a string is sequence of characters that is one of Python’s fundamental data types.
For example, name = input(“Enter a name”) the variable name is a string.
You might see the term string literal used, which is a string that appears in actual code of a program in contrast to the data type.
In the above example “Enter a name” is a string literal.
Often, the term literal is omitted and the word string is used both for the data type and actual character sequence. It is usually easy enough with context to distinguish between the two.



To append one string to the end of another string
Use the + operator to concatenate strings



message = 'Hello ' + 'world'

print(message)

Hello world



You can use string concatenation to break up a long string literal


print('Enter the amount of ' +

'sales for each day and ' +

'press Enter.')

Enter the amount of sales for each day and press Enter.


Notice how this statement is printed all on a single line.




Strings are immutable

Once they are created, they cannot be changed

Concatenation does not change the existing string, but rather creates a new string and assigns the new string to the previously used variable

We cannot use an expression of the form
string[index] = new_character

Statement like this that attempt to overwrite a part of the string will result in an error







An f-string (formatted string literal) is a special type of string literal that is prefixed with the letter f


print(f'Hello world')

Hello world



f-strings support placeholders for variables


name = 'Johnny'

print(f'Hello {name}.')

Hello Johnny.



Placeholders can also be expressions that are evaluated


print(f'The value is {10 + 2}.')

The value is 12.



val = 10

print(f'The value is {val + 2}.')

The value is 12.



Format specifiers can be used with placeholders


num = 123.456789

print(f'{num:.2f}')

123.46



2f means:

round the value to 2 decimal places
display the value as a floating-point number

Percentages


num = 1000000.00

print(f'{num:,.2f}')

1,000,000.00



discount = 0.5

print(f'{discount:.0%}')

50%



Scientific Notation


num = 123456789

print(f'{num:,d}')

123,456,789



num = 12345.6789

print(f'{num:.2e}')

1.23e+04



The order of designators in a format specifier

When using multiple designators in a format specifier, write them in this order:
[alignment][width][,][.precision][type]
Example: print(f'{number:^10,.2f}')


There are many other options and ways of formatting strings in Python. The office reference material at https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/inputoutput.html contains extensive details.




Strings in Python have many types of methods, divided into different types of operations

General format: mystring.method(arguments)

Some methods test a string for specific characteristics

Generally Boolean methods, that return True if a condition exists, and False otherwise


Some String Testing Methods







Method
Description




isalnum()
Returns true if the string contains only alphabetic letters or digits and is at least one character in length. Returns false otherwise.


isalpha()
Returns true if the string contains only alphabetic letters and is at least one character in length. Returns false otherwise.


isdigit()
Returns true if the string contains only numeric digits and is at least one character in length. Returns false otherwise.


islower()
Returns true if all of the alphabetic letters in the string are lowercase, and the string contains at least one alphabetic letter. Returns false otherwise.


isspace()
Returns true if the string contains only whitespace characters and is at least one character in length. Returns false otherwise. (Whitespace characters are spaces, newlines (\n), and tabs (\t).


isupper()
Returns true if all of the alphabetic letters in the string are uppercase, and the string contains at least one alphabetic letter. Returns false otherwise.




Some methods return a copy of the string, to which modifications have been made

Simulate strings as mutable objects

String comparisons are case-sensitive

Uppercase characters are distinguished from lowercase characters
lower and upper methods can be used for making case-insensitive string comparisons


Some String Modification Methods







Method
Description




lower()
Returns a copy of the string with all alphabetic letters converted to lowercase. Any character that is already lowercase, or is not an alphabetic letter, is unchanged.


lstrip()
Returns a copy of the string with all leading whitespace characters removed. Leading whitespace characters are spaces, newlines (\n), and tabs (\t) that appear at the beginning of the string.


lstrip(char)
The char argument is a string containing a character. Returns a copy of the string with all instances of char that appear at the beginning of the string removed.


rstrip()
Returns a copy of the string with all trailing whitespace characters removed. Trailing whitespace characters are spaces, newlines(\n), and tabs (\t) that appear at the end of the string.


rstrip(char)
The char argument is a string containing a character. The method returns a copy of the string with all instances of char that appear at the end of the string removed.


strip()
Returns a copy of the string with all leading and trailing whitespace characters removed.


strip(char)
Returns a copy of the string with all instances of char that appear at the beginning and the end of the string removed.


upper()
Returns a copy of the string with all alphabetic letters converted to uppercase. Any character that is already uppercase, or is not an alphabetic letter, is unchanged.




Programs commonly need to search for substrings
Several methods to accomplish this:

endswith(substring): checks if the string ends with substring

Returns True or False

startswith(substring): checks if the string starts with substring

Returns True or False

find(substring): searches for substring within the string

Returns lowest index of the substring, or if the substring is not contained in the string, returns -1

replace(substring, new_string):

Returns a copy of the string where every occurrence of substring is replaced with new_string



Some Search and Replace Methods







Method
Description




endswith(substring)
The substring argument is a string. The method returns true if the string ends with substring.


find (substring)
The substring argument is a string. The method returns the lowest index in the string where substring is found. If substring is not found, the method returns negative 1


replace(old, new)
The old and new arguments are both strings. The method returns a copy of the string with all instances of old replaced by new.


startswith (substring)
The substring argument is a string. The method returns true if the string starts with substring.







Repetition operator: makes multiple copies of a string and joins them together

The * symbol is a repetition operator when applied to a string and an integer

String is left operand; number is right

General format: string_to_copy * n
Variable references a new string which contains multiple copies of the original string






split method: returns a list containing the words in the string

By default, uses space as separator
Can specify a different separator by passing it as an argument to the split method



my_string = 'One two three four'

word_list = my_string.split()

print(word_list)

['One', 'two', 'three', 'four']



my_string = '1/2/3/4/5'

number_list = my_string.split('/')

print(number_list)

['1', '2', '3', '4', '5']






Sometimes a string contains substrings that are separated by a special character

Example: 'peach raspberry strawberry vanilla'

This string contains the substrings peach, raspberry, strawberry, and vanilla if we choose the space to be our separator.

The substrings are separated by the space character
The substrings are known as tokens and the separating character is known as the delimiter

The string '17;92;81;12;46;5' contains the tokens 17, 92, 81, 12, 46, and 5 if we choose the delimiter to be the ; character.
Tokenizing is the process of breaking a string into tokens

When you tokenize a string, you extract the tokens and store them as individual items
In Python you can use the split method to tokenize a string



str = 'peach raspberry strawberry vanilla'

tokens = str.split()

print(tokens)

['peach', 'raspberry', 'strawberry', 'vanilla']



my_address = 'www.example.com'

tokens = my_address.split('.')

print(tokens)

['www', 'example', 'com']

text:
Lists

The most common general purpose multidimensional variable in Python is the list.
Lists are ordered collections of values.

Duplicates are allowed.
You may have different types of data present in a single list.

We use the order built into a list to access and alter the different values.

title: 3: Strings, Lists and Tuples
text:
Creating a List

Lists are created using the square brackets [ ]
Separate multiple items in a list using a comma.


A_List = [ ] #This is an empty list

B_List = [ 1 , 2 ] #This list contains integers 1 and 2

text:
Accessing Elements in a List

Items within a list are often referred to as elements.
Use the square brackets [ ] after the name of the list to reference the location of the desired element.
Why ‘b’?

Python starts counting from 0.
Element 1 is then at the second position.



C_List = [ 'a' , 'b' , 'c' ]

print(C_List[1])

b



C_List = [ 'x' , 'y' , 'z' ]

print(C_List[0])

x

y

z

text:
Adding Elements to a List

Adding new elements to a list in Python is often accomplished using two methods.
The insert function adds an item to a specific index (location).

insert(index,value)


C_List = [ 'x' , 'y' , 'z' ]

C_List.insert(0,'a')

print(C_List)

['a', 'x', 'y', 'z']


The append function adds an item directly to the end of the list. Adding an item to the end of a list is a very common operation, so it was given its own dedicated function.

append(value)


C_List = [ 'x' , 'y' , 'z' ]

C_List.append('a')

print(C_List)

['x', 'y', 'z', 'a']

Removing an element at a specified index.

pop(index)

pop()


By omitting the index from the pop method, Python automatically assumes you want to remove the last item in the list.


C_List = [ 'x' , 'y' , 'z' ]

del[index]

Note that the del operation uses the square brackets instead of the parenthesis.
The del operation can also be used to completely delete a list.

del my_list

Span is a list containing copies of elements from start up to, but not including, end

Distance and the Feature Space

So far, we have viewed vectors as arrows in 2D or 3D physical space.
In modern computing, a vector is just a list of features.
If an object has 5 attributes, they can be viewed as a single point in a 5-Dimensional Vector Space.
While we cannot draw 5D space, the mathematics work the same.
The exact same NumPy addition and dot products we used for 2D apply to 5D or 10,000-dimensional data.

title: 16: Distance and Similarity

Distance and the Feature Space

A row in a DataFrame is just a point in a high-dimensional space.
The DataFrame below has a dimension of three, since it contains three features.

patients = pd.DataFrame({

})

title: 16: Distance and Similarity

The y-coordinate as heart rate.

How Close Are Two Data Points?

To find similar things, we measure the distance between their vectors.
The closer the distance, the more similar the objects are.
The question is, how to calculate the distance?

title: 16: Distance and Similarity
text:
Distance Measures

There are many ways to calculate the distance in a vector space.
We will talk about the two most commonly used methods.

Euclidean Distance (Straight-line Distance)
Manhattan Distance (City Block Distance)

Finding the Closest Match

How does a computer classify something new?

It finds the closest historical data point.

We will develop an algorithm to find the closest match in our DataFrame for a given point.

We need to iterate through every row in the DataFrame, as we will not know if there is a closer pair unless we examine every pair.
We then need to calculate the distance between each pair.
We will need to keep track of the smallest distance.

for _, row in df.iterrows():
d = np.linalg.norm(row.to_numpy() - unknown)
if d < smallest_distance:
smallest_distance = d
print(smallest_distance)

patients.to_numpy() - unknown,
axis=1 #this specifies we calculate across the columns

title: 16: Distance and Similarity
text:
Finding the Closest Match

What about finding the two closest points?
Most of our code can be reused, but we will need to keep track of the second smallest distance.

title: 16: Distance and Similarity

text:
Finding the Closest Match

What about finding the three closest points?
We now need to have conditions that handle:

the observation is the smallest overall

title: 4: Vectors and NumPy
text:
Lists and Vectors
Standard Python is designed for general software development, not math. Structures like lists in Python have their own set of rules that makes using them in mathematical operations difficult. If we try to perform math on a standard Python list, the results are either completely wrong for our purposes, or they crash the program.
Consider a list of test scores: scores = [85, 90, 78]
If we want to double the score of every student, our first instinct is to multiply the list by 2:

print(scores * 2)

But what happens is it repeats the list items

scores = [85, 90,  78]
print(scores * 2)

[85, 90, 78, 85, 90, 78]


Now, if we try to add 2 bonus points to every score using scores + 2, Python throws a TypeError because it does not understand how to combine a list with an integer.

title: 4: Vectors and NumPy
text:
Libraries

If we want mathematics to play well with the idea of lists, we need more specialized tools.
Libraries are external toolsets built that we can bring into our Python code.
For numerical data, the industry standard is NumPy (Numerical Python).
If you are working on a local machine, you likely need to install the library first using pip install numpy in your terminal.
Cloud environments like Colab usually have it pre-installed.


Standard Library Functions and the import Statement

Standard library: library of pre-written functions that comes with Python

Library functions perform tasks that programmers commonly need

Example: print, input, range
Viewed by programmers as a “black box”


Some library functions built into Python interpreter

To use, just call the function

Modules: files that stores functions of the standard library

Help organize library functions not built into the interpreter
Copied to computer when you install Python

To call a function stored in a module, need to write an import statement

Written at the top of the program
Format: import module_name




Importing NumPy

Once you have access to NumPy we need to use an import statement:


import numpy as np


We use as np as a standard convention.
It acts as a nickname so we do not have to type “numpy” every time we want to use one of its tools.

scores = [85, 90, 78]

text:
Scalars

The standard textbook definition of a scalar is “a quantity with magnitude but no direction.”
Another more useful definition when it comes to dealing with vectors is a scalar is a scaling factor.

It is a quantity that stretches or shrinks something else.

In Python: A scalar is a standard integer or float like x = 5.

title: 4: Vectors and NumPy
text:
Vectors
A vector is an ordered list of coordinates that gives us instructions on how to move through space. The dimensionality of the space is the number of values in the vector.
In math, v = [3, 2] means “start at the origin, go 3 units along the x-axis and 2 units along y-axis.” The vector v here has two elements and so the space the vector is in is 2-dimensional.
We can represent this in Python as a 1-dimensional NumPy array.

import numpy as np

v = np.array([3, 2])


Visually, we have:

Tail at the origin (0, 0)
Head at (3, 2)
Length = magnitude
Orientation = direction


Note that vectors are not tied to a location. We can have two vectors be equal (their components are all identical) while having a different origin.

title: 4: Vectors and NumPy
text:
Vector Arithmetic

Magnitude
The magnitude of a vector is its length.
We can find the magnitude of a vector v = [a, b, c, ...] by using the Euclidean distance |v| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + ...}
From the definition of the magnitude we can see that it is always non-negative and is a scalar value.


Example

Assume you walk 3m east then 4m north.
We can find the straight-line distance from your starting point to your destination using the magnitude of the sum of the vectors.
Since we are working in a 2-dimensional space this is just the Pythagorean theorem.


east= np.array([3,0])

north = np.array([0,4])

np.linalg.norm(east+north)

np.float64(5.0)




Addition and Subtraction
Adding (or subtracting) two vectors is combining their instructions.
This can be visualized with the “head to tail” method.


a = np.array([2, 1])

b = np.array([1, 3])

print(a + b)

[3 4]




Scalar Multiplication
Applying a positive scalar to a vector scales its magnitude (length) without changing its fundamental line of direction.
Applying a negative scalar scales its magnitude and changes the direction exactly 180 degrees.


v = np.array([3, 4])

print(2 * v)

[6 8]


Note that the vector in the code about is twice as long when scaled by 2.


Vector Multiplication
It is natural to assume that if you can do a + b then you can do a \times b. However, when it comes to vectors simply placing an \times between them is undefined. We need to specify exactly what we are calculating.
There are in fact three different ways to “multiply” vectors. These are not different ways to do the same thing, they are entirely different tools design to answer entirely different questions.


The Hadamard Product
In NumPy, the * operator is defined for vectors. That is, a * b will result in output. But it is not likely to be the output you wanted.

a = np.array([1, 2])

b = np.array([3, 4])

print(a * b)

[3 8]


This is the Hadamard product, which is used to scale the corresponding components of two vectors independently. The Hadamard product simply multiples matching elements:
[a,b] * [c,d] = [a*c, b*d]
That is, it performs element-wise multiplication.
Note that the output is a vector of the same dimensions as the inputs.
The Hadamard product is not often used because it depends on the coordinate system chosen (a choice which is often changed due to mathematical convenience).


The Dot Product
The dot product (or scalar product) is used to determine how much two vectors point in the same direction.
The dot product has two formulations (where |v| is the magnitude of the vector v)
a \cdot b = |a||b|\cos(\theta )
a \cdot b = a_1b_1 + a_2b_2 + ...
Note that the output of the dot product is a scalar (hence the term scalar product).

a = np.array([1, 2])

b = np.array([3, 4])

print(np.dot(a, b)) # print(a @ b) is equivalent

11


We can use the dot product to determine the projection of one vector onto another. Note that orthogonal (perpendicular) vectors have a dot product of zero.

We will use the dot product later in the course as it can be used to calculate the similarity between two objects that have a vector representation.


The Cross Product
The cross product finds the unique direction that is perpendicular to both of the vectors and its associated magnitude.
The output of the cross product is a vector itself.

This implies that we need at least a 3-dimensional space to work in.

If we take two vectors, they form a flat 2D pane. The cross product produces a new vector completely out of that pane, perpendicular to both.

The length (magnitude) of this new vector represents the area of the parallelogram formed by the original two vectors.

If the two vectors point in the exact same direction, their cross product is zero (no area, no leverage).
If they are perpendicular, the cross product is at its maximum.


a = np.array([4, 1, 0])

b = np.array([1, 4, 0])

# The cross product

print(np.cross(a, b))

[ 0  0 15]

title: 4: Vectors and NumPy
text:
Attributes in NumPy
Arrays in NumPy have certain inherent properties, called attributes, that can be useful for diagnosing errors or just inspecting the array. Note that attributes are different from functions, so they do not use parentheses () at the end.

array.shape
array.shape returns a tuple indicating the number of elements along each axis.

For a 1D array it returns (n,).
For a 2D array it returns (number of rows, number of columns).

Many operations involving vectors require equivalent shapes. For example, the dot product is defined only on two vectors of identical length. array.shape can be used to help diagnose or prevent errors like this.

prices = np.array([10, 20, 30])

print(prices.shape)# Output: (3,) A 1D array with 3 elements

grid = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4], [5, 6]])

print(grid.shape)# Output: (3, 2) 3 rows, 2 columns

(3,)
(3, 2)


Note that the comma in a 1D shape like (3,) is because Python handles tuples with a trailing comma to distinguish them from regular parentheses.

It means “3 elements in the first dimension, and no other dimensions exist.”



array.ndim
array.ndim returns the total number of dimensions (axes) that the array has.

A scalar has ndim = 0
A vector has ndim = 1
A matrix has ndim = 2



array.dtype
array.dtype tells you exactly what kind of data is stored inside.
This can be very useful as NumPy enforces uniform types. If a single string slips into your numbers, the whole array converts to text. Checking .dtype reveals if your numbers have become strings.

title: 4: Vectors and NumPy
text:
Common Functions in NumPy

Aggregates

Average: Takes the arithmetic mean of the array.

np.mean()

Sum: Adds up every element in the array.

np.sum()

Max: Returns the largest element in the array.

np.max()

Min: Returns the smallest element in the array.

np.min()




Reshape
array.reshape() changes the dimensions of an array without changing its actual data.

flat_data = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6])

# Morph it into 3 rows and 2 columns

grid_data = flat_data.reshape(3, 2)

print(grid_data)

[[1 2]
 [3 4]
 [5 6]]


Note that you cannot reshape an array into dimensions that do not fit the number of elements.
If you try flat_data.reshape(3, 3) on the above array, NumPy will throw a: ValueError: cannot reshape array of size 6 into shape (3,3). The shape (3,3) requires exactly 9 items, and we only have 6.


Flatten
array.flatten() takes a multi-dimensional grid and squashes it back down into a single 1D row. This iu Useful when a library expects a flat sequence of values, but you currently have them inside a multi-dimensional structure.

grid_data = np.array([[1, 2],[3, 4],[5, 6]])

# Morph it into 1 row

flat_data = grid_data.flatten()

print(flat_data)

[1 2 3 4 5 6]




isnan
np.isnan() returns a Boolean array (True/False) indicating where missing or corrupted data (NaN or Not a Number) is located.
If you run np.mean(scores)and the result is just NaN, having just a single broken data point has ruined your calculation. Combining this with an aggregate tool allows you to count how many broken points you have.

data = np.array([85, np.nan, 90])

# Find the missing data

print(np.isnan(data))

# Output: [False, True, False]

# Count how many missing values exist

print(np.sum(np.isnan(data)))

# Output: 1 (Because True acts as 1, False acts as 0)

[False  True False]
1




astype
array.astype() explicitly forces an array to convert from one data type to another.
If you read data from a file and it imports everything as text strings (e.g., ["10", "20", "30"]), you use astype to cast them into actual integers or floats so you can perform vector arithmetic.

string_scores = np.array(["85", "90", "78"])

# Fix the type so we can do math

numeric_scores = string_scores.astype(float)

print(numeric_scores * 2)

Indexing and Slicing
NumPy arrays use similar rules for accessing data as standard structures like Python lists. You do not need to relearn how to extract data. The exact same syntax works:

Indexing: scores[0] retrieves the first element.
Negative Indexing: scores[-1] retrieves the last element.
Slicing: scores[1:3] retrieves the second and third elements.

title: 6: Basic Plotting
text:
The matplotlib package is a library for creating two-dimensional charts and graphs. Like NumPy, it is not part of the standard Python library, so you will have to install it separately.
The matplotlib package contains a module named pyplot that you will need to import. Use the following import statement to import the module and create an alias named plt:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

Plotting in matplotlib is no different conceptually than using x, y coordinates on graph paper.
If you give matplotlib an array of X data points and an array of X data points, it pairs them up sequentially: (𝑥_0, 𝑦_0 ), (𝑥_1, 𝑦_1 ), … and draws a line between them.


To plot data, we first need some.

import numpy as np

x = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
y = x ** 2



Before we draw anything, we have to set up our canvas. In Matplotlib, this is done using the Object-Oriented API, which separates the window from the chart itself.
-The Figure (fig): The blank canvas that the plots will be drawn on. It controls global settings like size, background color, and layout. -The Axes (ax): The specific plot inside the figure. This contains the actual x and y axes, tick marks, labels, titles, and the data lines.
Note that there is a substantial number of examples that use the older plt.plot() style, which blends these two concepts together and requires one less line of code. While slightly faster for simple plots, it is much easier to use the figure and axis architecture when you want to customize things.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
plt.show()








We can see that we get a completely blank set of axes of 6 inches in width and 4 inches in height.
It is very important to avoid forgetting plt.show(). If you write all your ax.plot() code but forget plt.show() at the very end, Python will just silently finish running and show you nothing.
We now need to actually apply content to the axes to see our plot. We will use use ax.plot(x, y) to create a line plot.

ax.plot(x, y) 







A line plot is good for shwoing tends over time, distance, area, etc.

days = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
stock_price = np.array([150, 152, 149, 155, 158])

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(days, stock_price) # .plot() defaults to a line
plt.show()











Bar charts are suited for categorical comparisons.

products = np.array(["Software", "Hardware", "Consulting"])
revenue = np.array([50000, 35000, 20000])

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.bar(products, revenue)
plt.show()











Scatter plots are useful for seeing if two variables are correlated.

marketing_spend = np.array([1000, 2500, 1500, 4000, 3000])
new_customers = np.array([10, 22, 14, 45, 32])

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.scatter(marketing_spend, new_customers)
plt.show()












All of our previous plots are incomplete, as there is no context for what the visuals mean.

ax.set_title()

Sets the overall plot title.

ax.set_xlabel()

Sets the title for the x-axis.

ax.set_ylabel()

Sets the title for the y-axis.

ax.legend()

Enables the legend. You need to attach labels to the data form them to be displayed in the legend.


Adding context makes this scatter plot comprehensible.

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.scatter(marketing_spend, new_customers)
ax.set_title("Marketing Spend vs. New Customers")
ax.set_xlabel("New Customers")
ax.set_ylabel("Marketing Spend (1000$)")
plt.show()








Whenever we use methods like ax.set_title()or ax.set_xlabel(), we can pass optional arguments to change how the text looks.

fontsize : Accepts an integer representing the point size (e.g., 14), or relative text strings like ‘small’, ‘medium’, ‘large’.
fontweight : Sets the thickness of the font.

Most common choices are ‘normal’, ‘bold’, or ‘light’.

color: Changes the text color.

Matplotlib accepts standard names (‘red’, ‘black’), hexadecimal strings (‘#1e3a8a’), or grayscale floats (‘0.5’).

fontname : Allows changing the font family (e.g., ‘serif’, ‘sans-serif’).

These arguments go directly inside the plotting call itself (like ax.plot(), ax.scatter()). They change how the visual representation of the data is drawn.

color : The color of the line, markers, or bars.
linewidth : The thickness of a line plot (e.g., lw=2.5).
linestyle : The pattern of the line.

Common values are:

‘-’ (solid line)
‘–’ (dashed line)
‘:’ (dotted line)


alpha: Sets the transparency of the element.

It ranges from 0.0 (completely invisible) to 1.0 (completely opaque).
This is very useful when plotting overlapping datasets.

label: The name string associated with this specific data line.

This is what Matplotlib reads automatically when you call ax.legend().


There are many more options than what is listed here that can be found in the offical documentation.
This example combines many of these methods to make a plot that is easy to comprehend.

# Generate data
#linspace here creates a vector of 100 data points evenly spaced from 0 to 10 (inclusive).
x = np.linspace(0, 10, 100)
y1 = np.sin(x)
y2 = np.cos(x)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))

# Apply geometric styling to the data presentation

ax.plot(x, y1, color='blue', linestyle='-', linewidth=2, label='Sensor Alpha')
ax.plot(x, y2, color='darkorange', linestyle=':', linewidth=2.5, label='Sensor Beta')

# Apply text styling
# pad creates whitespace between the title text and the plot grid. 
ax.set_title("Sensor Comparison Analysis", fontsize=16, fontweight='bold', pad=15)
ax.set_xlabel("Duration (seconds)", fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
ax.set_ylabel("Signal Strength (mV)", fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')

#Styling the legend text and grid line structures

ax.legend(fontsize=11, loc='lower left')
ax.grid(True, linestyle='--', alpha=0.4, color='gray')

#linspace here creates a vector of 100 data points evenly spaced from 0 to 10 (inclusive).
x = np.linspace(0, 10, 100)
y1 = np.sin(x)
y2 = np.cos(x)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))

# Apply geometric styling to the data presentation

ax.plot(x, y1, color='blue', linestyle='-', linewidth=2, label='Sensor Alpha')
ax.plot(x, y2, color='darkorange', linestyle=':', linewidth=2.5, label='Sensor Beta')

# Apply text styling
# pad creates whitespace between the title text and the plot grid. 
ax.set_title("Sensor Comparison Analysis", fontsize=16, fontweight='bold', pad=15)
ax.set_xlabel("Duration (seconds)", fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
ax.set_ylabel("Signal Strength (mV)", fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')

#Styling the legend text and grid line structures

ax.legend(fontsize=11, loc='lower left')
ax.grid(True, linestyle='--', alpha=0.4, color='gray')

Object-oriented Programming

Object-oriented programming involves four key ideas: encapsulation, information hiding, inheritance, and polymorphism.
Encapsulation is the idea that a class can package some data together with the methods that manipulate the data.

This is a powerful capability, and the chief idea that distinguishes OOP from structured programming.

Information Hiding promotes quality code by allowing objects to protect their state against direct manipulation by code using the object.
Python, like many languages, provides mechanisms to achieve information hiding, but we do not cover them in this course.
Inheritance and polymorphism are mechanisms that help to enable code reuse and contract-based programming.

Now, suppose we want to create a class that works like Point in every respect, but also keeps track of a short description for the point.
We could create a LabeledPoint class by copying and pasting the definition for Point, changing the name to LabeledPoint, and modifying the class to suit our purposes.
However, any time you copy and paste code, keep in mind that you are copying and pasting bugs that may exist in the code.
Inheritance provides a way to reuse the definition of Point without having to copy and paste.

class LabeledPoint(Point):
def __init__(self, initX, initY, label):
self.x = initX
self.y = initY
self.label = label
def __str__(self):
return “x=” + str(self.x) + “, y=” + str(self.y) + ” (” + self.label + “)”

An assignment is the process that is used to create a variable and make it reference data (or reference different data if the variable already exists).
The general format of an assignment statement is:

The general format for assignment is:
variable_name = expression

For example:

This sets the variable mass to the value 50.
Be careful not to confuse the assignment operator = with the equals sign. In Python, this symbol is used for assignment. When we reach conditional statements in the future, we will see that the equality operator (which asks the questions are two objects equal) is the double equals sign ==.
Note that in our examples, the variable receiving the value is always on the left side. This is a general rule in Python, the variable that takes on the value must be on the left.
We also can only use a variable if there is a value actually assigned to it.
number = 
The code above here is broken, as the variable named number is not assigned to anything. This will cause a syntax error.


You can also assign values to multiple variables in a single statement. This is known as multiple assignment.
The following code blocks are functionally equivalent:

The purpose of data types is to categorize the value located in memory.
The major types in Python are: - int for integer - float for a real number - str for sequences of characters (these can be any kind of symbol from letters to numbers to punctuation and more) - bool for Boolean values (True or False)

7

With more complex data types (like lists which will be introduced soon), variables behave differently.
The assignment shares access to the same data. The variable names point to a location that holds a single instance of the data. If you change the data through one variable, it will be reflected to all the other variables that point at the same underlying data.
For simple types (int, float, str, bool) assignment copies the value.
For complex types (lists and many others) assignment shares access to the same data.



Python has a set of rules for naming variables. Most of these if ignored will result in a syntax error.

Variable name cannot be a Python keyword
Variable name cannot contain spaces
First character must be a letter or an underscore
After first character may use letters, digits, or underscores
Variable names are case sensitive

In general, a variable’s name should reflect its use. This makes finding and fixing problems in your code much easier. Note that it is common for certain variables to have very simple names (i, j, k, etc.) when they are used for certain common operations. When starting out, you may want to use a more descriptive name to help your understanding.

Also, in Python, you do not need to worry about deleting variables after they have been used (like some other programming languages). Values that are no longer referenced by variables are automatically removed by Python’s garbage collector.

A magic number is an unexplained numeric value that appears in a program’s code.
For example:
amount = balance * 0.065
The value 0.065 is not specified as to what it actually is. It could be an interest rate, or a fee percentage, or many other possible things. Only the person who wrote the code knows for sure (assuming they remember).
If a magic number is used in many places in a program it can take substantial effort to find and change the number in each location. You take the risk of making a mistake each type you type the magic number the program’s code. This can be the source of difficult to find and frustrating errors.


Rather than using magic numbers, you should used a variable whose purpose is to represent the value. This variable is not intended to be changed during the program and so is called a constant. In practice, Python will allow you to change the value, so it is important to remember that this variable is supposed to be static. The common convention in Python is to use all caps to indicate a constant variable.

INTEREST_RATE = 0.051





None is a special Python value that represents no value assigned yet. Note that None is a value (not an error). Its data type is a unique NoneType.
None is used as a placeholder when a value is unknown or not available.
None is not the same as: - 0 (a number) - “” (an empty string) - False (a Boolean)
We use None to: - Initialize a variable before it has a real value - Represent missing or unknown information - Indicate that a result has not been computed yet
Rule to remember: Do not perform math or string operations on None. - Any of these operations causes an error.

The Print Function
We have already seen the print function in the Hello World example. The print function will be one of the most commonly used functions throughout this course. It is extremely useful when trying to debug code, as you can see the contents of variables as your program progresses through its instructions.

Program Execution Order
In general, statements execute in the order that they appear. Specifically, the go from top (first) to bottom (last). In the future we will see ways of repeating or skipping sections of code.
The output of the following example is ‘one’ then ‘two’ then ‘three’.

print('one')
print('two')
print('three')

one
two
three




Displaying Multiple Items with the Print Function
Python allows one to display multiple items with a single call to print. - Items are separated by commas when passed as arguments. - Arguments displayed in the order they are passed to the function. - Items are automatically separated by a space when displayed on screen.

print('one', 'two', 'three')

one two three


Based off the previous examples we can see that successive print statements place their value(s) on different lines. This is because the print function puts a newline character at the end of printed data. We can change this default newline to a value of our choice using the special argument end.
The following example changes the default newline to a space.

print('one',end=' ')
print('two',end=' ')
print('three',end=' ')

one two three 


Similarly, for multiple items displayed on the same line, we can use the separator argument sep to change the default space to something else.
The following example changes the default space to a dash.

print('one', 'two', 'three',sep='-')

one-two-three


Both of these options can be useful to help format printed values to make reading their output easier.


Newlines and Tabs
Certain special characters are preceded by a backslash \.
These characters are treated as commands inside a string.
To create a newline, we use the character \n.
Note the extra new line in the following example.

print('Hello world\n')
print('Hello world')

Hello world

Hello world


To create a tab, we use \t.
Note the increased whitespace (the tab character) between the words Hello and world.

print('Hello\tworld')

Hello   world


We can also see that there is no additional space here in the string Hello\tworld and yet the tab is still correctly placed. If we included space between the tab and the other parts of the string like:

print('Hello \t world')

Hello    world


We see that there is additional space in the printed output. This is an important feature of printing strings in that anything inside the string is printed exactly as it is written. By adding the spaces to make things easier for us to read inside the string, we altered the output.

More complicated kinds of input tend to require more effort to both read and process, so we will avoid these in an introductory course.
The input function displays an optional prompt and then reads input from the keyboard.

variable_name = input("Your Prompt Here")

Note that the input function always returns the data as a string.
The prompt is typically a string instructing user to enter a value.
The input function also does not automatically display a space after the prompt.
For example:
name = input("What is your name?  ")
The above does the following:

Displays the string ‘What is your name?’
Reads input, as a string, from the keyboard
Assigns the string that was read from the keyboard to the name variable


Reading Numbers with the Input Function
Since the input function always returns a string, if we want to use the input as a number in calculations we will need to cast the string to the appropriate numerical type.
number = int(input('Enter a number: '))
The above does the following:

Displays the string ‘Enter a number:’
Reads input, as a string, from the keyboard
Converts the input to an int
Assigns the resulting int to the number variable

Matrix multiplication is unlike scalar multiplication which is commutative (order does not matter). Multiplication of two matrices is defined only if both have a relation between their dimensions. Specifically, the first matrix must have the same number of columns as the second matrix has rows.
In NumPy we can use the shape attribute to find the dimensions of a matrix.
A.shape here returns (2,3)

Two rows, three columns


A = np.array([
[1, 2, 3],
[4, 5, 6]
])

print(A.shape)

(2, 3)


These conventions are the same as in linear algebra.

Rows run horizontally
Columns run vertically

A 2\times 3 matrix is understood to have 2 rows and 3 columns.
